entry.title: [qs] qs : qs.stringify with arrayFormat 'comma' throws an uncaught TypeError on array elements carrying a non-callable own toString (DoS)
entry.content:
Summary

qs.stringify(obj, { arrayFormat: 'comma' }) throws an uncaught TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value when an array in obj contains an element that carries an own, non-callable toString property (for example { a: [ { toString: 'x' } ] }). A remote, unauthenticated attacker who can influence an object that the application later re-serializes with the comma array format triggers the throw. In a service that lacks a synchronous error boundary around the serialization call, the uncaught exception crashes the worker process, producing a denial of service.

Root Cause

When arrayFormat: 'comma' is selected, the comma branch collapses the whole array into a single value via Array.prototype.join, or, under encodeValuesOnly: true, maps each element through the value encoder before joining. Both paths perform an implicit string coercion (ToPrimitive with hint "string") on each element. For an object whose own toString is a non-callable value, coercion skips the shadowed non-callable toString, falls through to Object.prototype.valueOf (which returns the object rather than a primitive), and throws. The comma branch runs this coercion before the per-element null and skip handling in the main loop, so nothing downstream can neutralize the hostile element, and the throw is never caught inside the library.

lib/stringify.js  (comma-array branch)
  line 152-154: obj = utils.maybeMap(obj, function (v) { return v == null ? v : encoder(v); });  // encodeValuesOnly path
  line 156:     objKeys = [{ value: obj.length > 0 ? obj.join(',') || null : void undefined }];   // default comma path
lib/utils.js
  line 292:     string = String(str);   // value encoder coercion reached via the encodeValuesOnly path

Impact

Prerequisites: the application calls qs.stringify with arrayFormat: 'comma' (a documented, supported option) on an object whose shape can be influenced by attacker input. Attacker-controllable sources include qs.parse(input, { allowPrototypes: true }), which retains a toString segment (Express 4's default query parser, Express 5's extended query parser, and body-parser's extended urlencoded parser all set it), qs.parse(input, { plainObjects: true }), whose null-prototype elements throw even without a toString key (eg, a[][b]=c), and JSON.parse of a request body, which needs no qs parse option at all. No authentication or user interaction is required. Demonstrated capability: a single request forces an uncaught synchronous TypeError in the serialization call. In a naive single-process Node service with no synchronous error boundary, this crashes the process and takes the service offline (availability impact). Under a framework such as Express that traps synchronous handler throws, the plausible outcome is a per-request 500 rather than a full outage; that lower-impact case is noted but not the worst credible supported deployment. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact, no memory unsafety, and no prototype pollution.

Proof of Concept

Install qs at the affected version (for example 6.16.0) and run the following script with Node.js. No network setup is required; it demonstrates the throw in isolation.

var qs = require('qs');

// Source A: qs.parse with allowPrototypes retains the hostile toString segment
qs.stringify(qs.parse('a[0][toString]=x', { allowPrototypes: true }), { arrayFormat: 'comma' });

// Source B: a JSON request body, no qs parse option needed
qs.stringify(JSON.parse('{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}'), { arrayFormat: 'comma' });

// Also affected: the encodeValuesOnly sub-path
qs.stringify(JSON.parse('{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}'), { arrayFormat: 'comma', encodeValuesOnly: true });

A default-join (allowPrototypes) => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
B default-join (JSON.parse) => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
C encodeValuesOnly path => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
N2 callable toString => NO THROW; output="a=z"
N3 isBuffer vector (CVE-2026-82417) => NO THROW; output="a%5Bconstructor%5D%5BisBuffer%5D=x"
qs version: 6.16.0

Attack Chain

  1. Exposure: A remote, unauthenticated request reaches an endpoint whose handler eventually serializes attacker-influenced data with qs.stringify(obj, { arrayFormat: 'comma' }).
  2. Control: The attacker supplies data that becomes { a: [ { toString: <non-callable value> } ] }, either via a[0][toString]=x parsed with allowPrototypes, or via a JSON body {"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}.
  3. Path: In stringify, the primitive/buffer guard at lib/stringify.js:134 is false for an array, so control reaches the comma branch at lib/stringify.js:149.
  4. Guard: On the encodeValuesOnly path, the closure v == null ? v : encoder(v) at lib/stringify.js:152-154 passes only null/undefined through; a non-null object still reaches the encoder. The default path skips that closure entirely and reaches obj.join(',') at lib/stringify.js:156 with no guard at all.
  5. Primitive: The element is coerced to a string (Array.prototype.join, or String(str) at lib/utils.js:292). ToPrimitive skips the non-callable own toString, valueOf returns the object, and a TypeError is thrown.
  6. Result: The uncaught synchronous exception propagates out of the serialization call, failing the request and, in a service without a synchronous error boundary, crashing the process (denial of service).

Bypass Evidence

This is a different element type on the code path CVE-2026-8723 (GHSA-q8mj-m7cp-5q26) patched, plus the default comma path, which that fix never covered. CVE-2026-8723 addressed a TypeError crash on null/undefined entries in the comma plus encodeValuesOnly path. Its fix (commit 21f80b3) wraps the encoder in function (v) { return v == null ? v : encoder(v); }, so it only passes null and undefined through. A non-null element with a hostile own toString fails the v == null test, so the encoder still runs and still throws; the encodeValuesOnly case (case C above) throws on the exact fixed code. The default comma path (encodeValuesOnly unset, the library default) never entered that fix at all: git log -S "obj.join(','" -- lib/stringify.js shows no security fix has ever touched the obj.join(',') line, and cases A and B throw with encodeValuesOnly unset. The related isBuffer hardening for CVE-2026-82417 (commit e83d321) is a different sink at the lib/stringify.js:134 guard, which is never entered for the array element; the negative control {a:{constructor:{isBuffer:'x'}}} serializes cleanly. Disproof attempts that failed: a valueOf-only object does not throw (it serializes to [object Object]), confirming the trigger is an element with no callable toString (an own non-callable toString, or a null-prototype object with no toString at all, as qs.parse produces under plainObjects); nested arrays ({"a":[[{"toString":"x"}]]}) throw the same way; a callable toString serializes cleanly; and the default (non-comma) array format serializes cleanly, confirming the comma format is required. All positive and negative cases were reproduced on the exact published 6.16.0 artifact.

Affected Versions

  • Ecosystem: npm
  • Package: qs
  • Confirmed affected range: >= 6.7.0, <= 6.16.0
  • Latest release checked: 6.16.0 (npm latest; git tag v6.16.0)
  • Fix status: fixed in 6.16.1 (a952e75)

The arrayFormat: 'comma' join sink was introduced in qs 6.7.0, so 6.7.0 is the lower boundary; releases before 6.7.0 lack the sink. No released version fixes this vector, and the latest published release (6.16.0) reproduces the throw, so the closed upper bound <= 6.16.0 covers every affected release. The encodeValuesOnly sub-path was added later, but the default comma-join vector already affects 6.7.0, so 6.7.0 governs the lower boundary.

Suggested Fix

The comma array serialization must not allow an implicit string coercion of an array element to throw an uncaught exception. Coercion of each comma element should be performed defensively (for example by wrapping the join and per-element encode so that a coercion failure is caught and handled), and this protection must cover both the default obj.join(',') path and the encodeValuesOnly encoder path, not only the previously patched null/undefined case. As an interim mitigation without a code change, applications can avoid arrayFormat: 'comma' when serializing data derived from untrusted input, sanitize parsed objects (avoid allowPrototypes/plainObjects on untrusted input and strip unexpected own properties), or wrap qs.stringify calls in a synchronous error boundary so a coercion failure cannot crash the process.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

Independent report by @Lucidsec

The following was reported separately, after this advisory, and is merged here as a duplicate.

Summary

In project qs, in versions >= 6.7.0, <= 6.16.0 (every version that supports arrayFormat: 'comma'), qs.stringify with arrayFormat: 'comma' can throw an uncaught TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value when an array element has a non-callable own toString. It is fixed in 6.16.1. Related: CWE-248 and CWE-704.

Technical Details

qs.stringify with arrayFormat: 'comma' joins an array at lib/stringify.js:156 via obj.join(','). An element whose own toString is not callable makes Array.prototype.join throw. There is no type check and no catch on that path.

A second path exists with encodeValuesOnly: at lib/stringify.js:151-154, maybeMap only skips v == null, then lib/utils.js:292 does String(str) and throws the same TypeError (this second site exists since v6.11.1; before that, the same input throws at join).

Who can trigger: someone who can shape an array element passed to stringify. The host must use non-default arrayFormat: 'comma'. Default arrayFormat indices does not fold arrays and is not affected. A parse-then-stringify path also needs plainObjects: true (null-prototype elements from lib/parse.js:200) or allowPrototypes: true (which Express 4's default query parser, Express 5's extended query parser, and body-parser's extended urlencoded parser all set). Default qs.parse('a[0][toString]=x') returns {} because the prototype guard drops toString. Direct JSON handed to stringify can supply {"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}.

Cause: the comma fold at lib/stringify.js:149-156 collapses the array into a single value before the main loop at lib/stringify.js:172-212, so skipNulls and strictNullHandling only ever see the joined value, never individual elements. isNonNullishPrimitive / isBuffer at lib/stringify.js:134 inspect the whole value, not each element. A normal object uses Object.prototype.toString and becomes [object Object]. An own non-callable toString is skipped, valueOf returns the object, and join throws. (The skipped TODO test at test/stringify.js:684-689 uses a plain { b: 1 } element, which does not throw; it covers the separate question of what comma format should output for object elements, not this crash.) Earlier comma crash fixes did not cover object elements.

Impact

One small input makes that serialization path throw a synchronous, catchable TypeError. Behind a framework error boundary (eg, a synchronous Express handler), the request fails with a 500 and the process survives. In a host with no error boundary (eg, a bare http.createServer handler), the uncaught exception exits the process (the client sees ECONNRESET). Availability only.

Proof of Concept

Show the proof of concept

Checked on the latest commit that was checked: 07b1d4d82c8f9301c105ea4b94fa2302cfd6e8b4. Still present. Demonstrated.

  • Payload {"a":[{"toString":"x"}]} throws at lib/stringify.js:156.
  • Baseline {"a":["x","y"]} returns 200 with body a=x%2Cy.
  • A plain object element stringifies to a=%5Bobject%20Object%5D and does not throw.
  • encodeValuesOnly: true throws via utils.js:292.
  • plainObjects parse plus comma throws.

Suggested Fix

Before join, map elements with the existing primitive check; skip or replace non-primitives so join cannot throw. On the encodeValuesOnly path, do not send non-primitives into String(). Optionally guard lib/utils.js:292. Add new regression tests.

References

entry.title: [hbs] hbs: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Externally-Accessible File or Directory and Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
entry.content:
The npm hbs package is an Express view engine wrapper for Handlebars. Depending on usage, users of hbs may be vulnerable to a file disclosure vulnerability. There is currently no patch for this vulnerability. hbs mixes pure template data with engine configuration options through the Express render API. By overwriting internal configuration options a file disclosure vulnerability may be triggered in downstream applications. For an example PoC see the referenced GHSL-2021-020.

entry.title: [undici] undici WebSocket client vulnerable to Denial of Service via failed HTTP/2 handshake
entry.content:
Impact

undici's experimental WebSocket client (enabled by default via allowH2: true) crashes the Node.js process when it connects to a malicious server over HTTP/2. If the server answers the WebSocket upgrade with a response that fails handshake validation, undici aborts the request, but the abort is a no-op because the request is already marked completed, so the underlying ClientHttp2Stream is left open with no error listener. When the server then destroys the connection, the orphaned stream emits an unhandled error and the process exits. A remote, unauthenticated server can therefore deny service to any client that opens a WebSocket to it over HTTP/2. undici 8.11.0 and 8.11.1 are affected; the regression was introduced in 8.11.0.

Patches

Upgrade to 8.11.2.

Workarounds

Set allowH2: false to disable HTTP/2 for WebSocket connections, or avoid opening WebSocket connections to untrusted servers, until upgrading.

References

entry.title: [git-diff] git-diff: OS command injection vulnerability via crafted strings to the gitDiff API
entry.content:
git-diff before 2.0.7 contains an OS command injection vulnerability that allows attackers to execute shell commands by supplying crafted strings to the gitDiff API. Attackers who control a diffed document string can embed $(cmd) or backtick substitutions that shelljs.exec evaluates, running commands with Node.js process privileges.

entry.title: [better-auth] @better-auth/drizzle-adapter: Concurrent requests can exceed rate limits on PostgreSQL
entry.content:
Am I affected?

You are affected if you use @better-auth/drizzle-adapter from 1.6.17 through versions before 1.7.7 (including the 1.7.0 prereleases from beta.6 through rc.6) or @better-auth/kysely-adapter 1.6.17 through 1.6.31, and keep rate-limit records in a PostgreSQL database.

All of these must be true:

  • Rate limiting is enabled.
  • Rate-limit records are stored in the database.
  • The database is PostgreSQL, used through one of the adapter versions above.

You are not affected if you store rate-limit records in memory (the default) or in secondary storage.

Summary

Database-backed rate limiting on PostgreSQL can let a burst of concurrent requests go over the configured maximum. When many requests arrive at the same time, several of them can pass the limit check together. This weakens the rate limit on password sign-in, two-factor verification, one-time codes, password resets, and other rate-limited endpoints.

Impact

An attacker who sends many requests at once can make more attempts than the application allows.

The issue does not bypass password or one-time-code validation. It does not directly compromise an account. The number of extra attempts is limited by the number of concurrent database connections, the number of application instances, and the rate-limit window.

Patches

@better-auth/kysely-adapter is fixed in 1.7.0. Upgrade to 1.7.0 or later.

The Drizzle fix is merged for the planned @better-auth/drizzle-adapter 1.7.7 release. That package is not available yet. Upgrade better-auth and the installed Drizzle adapter together when 1.7.7 is available. No database schema or public API migration is required.

Workarounds

  • Store rate-limit records in secondary storage.
  • Use a custom rate-limit storage that checks and increments the counter in one atomic step. An atomic step cannot be interrupted by another request.
  • Enforce the intended limit at an upstream layer, such as a reverse proxy or gateway.

In-memory storage also avoids this issue. However, each application instance keeps its own counter, so it may not enforce one shared limit in multi-instance or serverless deployments.

References

  • https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/security/advisories/GHSA-44jh-23m7-hpcf
  • https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/11331
  • https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/commit/35d7cd389220f99cfc98ac699e6a42b48313a740
  • https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/releases/tag/v1.7.7
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-44jh-23m7-hpcf

entry.title: [better-auth] better-auth: OAuth Proxy lets an attacker sign in as another user
entry.content:
Am I affected?

You may be affected if you use better-auth from 1.5.0-beta.12 through versions before 1.7.7 with the OAuth Proxy plugin. You are affected only if all of these are also true:

  • On a participating environment, the OAuth Proxy plugin has no dedicated secret, or its secret equals that environment's global Better Auth secret.
  • Sign-in state is stored in a cookie (account.storeStateStrategy: "cookie"). With a database or secondary storage, this is only the case if you chose it explicitly.
  • Implicit account linking is on (the default).

You are not affected by this path if every participating environment uses a proxy secret distinct from its global Better Auth secret, if sign-in state is stored in the database, or if you use a version before 1.5.0-beta.12.

Summary

The OAuth Proxy plugin trusts any user profile it can decrypt. In the affected setup, Better Auth encrypts sign-in state, including data the caller chose, with the same secret and hands it to anyone who starts a social sign-in. An attacker can use this to get a fake profile for another user's email address that the proxy accepts as real.

Impact

An attacker without an account who knows a user's verified email address can sign in as that user, with that user's permissions. They can read private data, change the account, and link a provider account of their choice to it. They need no provider sign-in and no action from the victim. No availability impact is established, and a reported open redirect was not confirmed.

Patches

The fix is merged for the planned better-auth 1.7.7 release. That package is not available yet.

Upgrade all nodes handling the same cookie-backed OAuth or SAML state flow and all OAuth Proxy participants together, including the production coordinator and preview or development deployments. Keep installed Better Auth packages released alongside better-auth on the same release version. Restart pending sign-in and account-linking flows; pre-upgrade state cookies and proxy payloads are rejected. Public options and API signatures are unchanged.

Workarounds

Until you upgrade to the fixed release, apply one of these:

  • Set one strong OAuth Proxy secret across every environment that takes part in the proxy flow, and keep it different from each environment's global Better Auth secret.
  • Set account.storeStateStrategy: "database". This is already the default when a database or secondary storage is configured. If Magic Link is also enabled, switching can expose a separate cross-purpose verification-record path in affected releases. Ensure the two flows resolve to distinct stored identifiers; with built-in options, use Magic Link storeToken: "hashed" with global verification.storeIdentifier unset or "plain", or disable Magic Link or both built-in social and Generic OAuth sign-in.
  • Remove the OAuth Proxy plugin if you do not need it.

Setting account.accountLinking.disableImplicitLinking: true stops this path from taking over an existing account. It does not fix the underlying flaw: the callback can still accept attacker-made data as a provider identity. Apply one of the steps above as well.

References

  • https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/11494

entry.title: [better-auth] better-auth: OAuth state can be used as a Magic Link to sign in as another user
entry.content:
Am I affected?

You may be affected if you use better-auth from 1.4.0-beta.18 through versions before 1.7.7 with the Magic Link plugin and social or Generic OAuth sign-in.

You are affected if all of these are true:

  • Magic Link is enabled with default storeToken: "plain", or with storeToken: "hashed" and global verification.storeIdentifier: "hashed" (including a hashed default).
  • At least one built-in social provider or Generic OAuth provider is enabled.
  • OAuth state uses account.storeStateStrategy: "database", the default when a database or secondary storage is configured.

Cookie-backed state blocks this path, subject to the OAuth Proxy condition below. With custom hashers, confirm the flows cannot resolve to the same stored identifier.

Summary

Better Auth accepts an OAuth sign-in state value as a Magic Link token. An attacker can start an OAuth sign-in with any email address and use the returned state value to finish a Magic Link sign-in for that address. They never prove that they can read that email.

Impact

An unauthenticated attacker who knows a user's email address can get a normal session for that user, with all of that account's permissions. They need no access to the mailbox, and they do not need to sign in with the OAuth provider or complete an OAuth callback.

If Magic Link sign-up is enabled and no user has the email address, the attacker can instead create an account that Better Auth wrongly marks as email verified, and is signed in to it. The false verified-email flag can also bypass Better Auth's default unproven-account protections when the mailbox owner later signs in, leaving the attacker's session in that account. Applications that trust verified email addresses or email domains may give this account more access, depending on the application.

Patches

The fix is merged for the planned better-auth 1.7.7 release. That package is not available yet.

Upgrade better-auth and installed Better Auth adapters, plugins, and integrations released alongside it together. Upgrade servers sharing verification storage in the same cutover. Request new Magic Links and restart pending OAuth or SAML sign-ins; links and state created before the upgrade cannot complete. Update custom verification.storeIdentifier.overrides rules to match the magic-link: and auth-state: prefixes. There is no user or account data migration, and public token values and API signatures are unchanged.

Workarounds

Until you upgrade to the fixed release, use one of these mitigations:

  • Set account.storeStateStrategy to "cookie". If you also use OAuth Proxy, first configure one dedicated OAuth Proxy secret across all participating environments that differs from each environment's global Better Auth secret. Cookie-backed state can expose a separate OAuth Proxy account-takeover path when the proxy shares the global secret and implicit account linking is enabled.
  • Set the Magic Link plugin option storeToken to "hashed" and leave global verification.storeIdentifier unset or set it to "plain". Global identifier hashing does not prevent this issue when Magic Link tokens are also hashed.
  • Turn off Magic Link sign-in, or turn off social and Generic OAuth sign-in.

Setting disableSignUp: true on the Magic Link plugin is not enough. It only stops the creation of new verified accounts. It does not stop the takeover of existing accounts.

References

  • https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/security/advisories/GHSA-965c-763c-88jm
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-114607
  • https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/11494
  • https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/commit/ac54bfd67821a7607533af2059858b12bc54e26a
  • https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/releases/tag/v1.7.7
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-965c-763c-88jm

entry.title: [nodemailer] Nodemailer: Quadratic backtracking in SMTP AUTH mechanism detection regexes allows pre-auth remote denial of service
entry.content:
Summary

Nodemailer's SMTP client applies four regular expressions to a peer's EHLO response to detect the supported SASL mechanisms. Each pattern uses an alternation with two overlapping whitespace-matching sub-patterns, which produces quadratic (O(n^2)) backtracking whenever the mechanism name is absent from the line. A malicious or MITM SMTP server that answers EHLO with 250-AUTH followed by a long whitespace-only run and a non-matching token blocks the Node.js event loop for tens of seconds to hours during a pre-authentication handshake. No authentication to the target SMTP server is required, and any application that connects to an attacker-influenced host is affected.

Root Cause

Each of the four AUTH mechanism regexes in SMTPConnection._actionEHLO contains the sub-pattern (?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=) before the mechanism literal. [^\n]* and the trailing \s+ both match whitespace and can consume the same characters, so when the mechanism literal is absent, the regex engine must try every partition of the whitespace run between [^\n]* and \s+ before failing. The four regexes run unconditionally on every EHLO response, with no length cap, no shape validation, and no early rejection before the engine enters the ambiguous alternation.

Component: nodemailer (npm), SMTP client
Function:  SMTPConnection._actionEHLO
Location:  src/smtp-connection/index.ts, lines 2162, 2167, 2172, 2177
Patterns:  /[ -]AUTH(?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=)PLAIN/i
           /[ -]AUTH(?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=)LOGIN/i
           /[ -]AUTH(?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=)CRAM-MD5/i
           /[ -]AUTH(?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=)XOAUTH2/i

Impact

Algorithmic-complexity denial of service against any Node.js process that opens an SMTP connection to an attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced host. Node.js is single threaded, so the process stalls entirely while the regex engine backtracks: no other requests are served, no timers fire, and the built-in socket timeout (10 minutes) cannot interrupt synchronous JavaScript. A 4,000-character whitespace run inside a single continuation line already blocks each regex for tens of seconds; the client bounds a response at 1 MB, which leaves headroom for blocking runs measured in hours across the four patterns. Two realistic attacker positions reach the sink pre-authentication: a hosted mailer that lets tenants configure their own SMTP server, and any network-adjacent attacker able to man-in-the-middle a cleartext SMTP connection (including before STARTTLS negotiation).

Proof of Concept

The PoC exercises the exact four regexes copied from src/smtp-connection/index.ts against a synthesized 250-AUTH<whitespace>NOMATCH line, so no live SMTP server is needed to reproduce the timing.

Runtime:      Node.js >= 20
Dependencies: none
Invocation:   node poc.js

'use strict';

const AUTH_REGEXES = [
    /[ -]AUTH(?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=)PLAIN/i,
    /[ -]AUTH(?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=)LOGIN/i,
    /[ -]AUTH(?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=)CRAM-MD5/i,
    /[ -]AUTH(?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=)XOAUTH2/i,
];

function bench(n) {
    const line = '250-AUTH' + ' '.repeat(n) + 'NOMATCH';
    const start = Date.now();
    for (const re of AUTH_REGEXES) re.test(line);
    return Date.now() - start;
}

for (const n of [500, 1000, 2000, 3000]) {
    console.log(`n=${n}  four-regex time=${bench(n)} ms`);
}

const control = '250-AUTH PLAIN LOGIN CRAM-MD5 XOAUTH2';
const t0 = Date.now();
for (const re of AUTH_REGEXES) re.test(control);
console.log(`well-formed control  four-regex time=${Date.now() - t0} ms`);

n=500   four-regex time=914 ms
n=1000  four-regex time=1348 ms
n=2000  four-regex time=10558 ms
n=3000  four-regex time=35251 ms
well-formed control  four-regex time=0 ms

Doubling the whitespace run multiplies the wall time by roughly four, which matches the expected O(n^2) growth. The well-formed control shows that a normal EHLO response is parsed in effectively zero time.

Attack Chain

  1. Exposure: The victim application, or any dependent that uses nodemailer to send mail, opens a TCP or TLS connection to an SMTP host the attacker controls. This happens automatically for multi-tenant mailers whose tenants configure their own outbound SMTP server, and for any client whose plaintext SMTP session can be intercepted by a network-adjacent attacker before STARTTLS negotiation.
  2. Control: The attacker fully controls the bytes returned in response to EHLO. In particular, the attacker chooses the length and content of every 250- continuation line up to the client's 1 MB response cap.
  3. Path: Socket bytes are reassembled by _onData, decoded by _processResponse, and dispatched to _actionEHLO. On the first EHLO after the greeting (malicious server with no STARTTLS), on the second EHLO after a successful STARTTLS upgrade, or on the first EHLO when ignoreTLS is set, control reaches the AUTH detection block near the end of _actionEHLO.
  4. Guard: The only bounds on this path are maxResponseSize (1 MB by default) and the 421 or non-2xx status-code check. Neither prevents O(n^2) backtracking: 4,000 whitespace characters already block each regex for tens of seconds, well below the 1 MB cap. No length, shape, or sanitization check runs before the regexes.
  5. Primitive: Four RegExp.prototype.test calls execute against the crafted line, each entering catastrophic backtracking because [^\n]* and \s+ share the whitespace alphabet and the mechanism literal never matches.
  6. Result: The Node.js event loop is blocked for the duration of the four regex evaluations. All other work in the process, including timers, unrelated requests, keep-alive traffic, and the SMTP socket timeout itself, is suspended until the regexes return.

Bypass Evidence

The only response-side protection in this code path is maxResponseSize, introduced by the fix for GHSA-4g23-2xm8-66gc (commit f2d82fa). That fix targeted quadratic reassembly of long multiline replies inside _onData and left the AUTH regex evaluation in _actionEHLO untouched. maxResponseSize does not prevent this issue: at 4,000 whitespace characters, roughly 0.4 percent of the default 1 MB cap, a single continuation line already blocks each of the four regexes for tens of seconds. No status-code or length gate rejects the payload before the regex engine enters the ambiguous alternation, and Node.js's single-threaded event loop cannot service the socket timeout while a synchronous test() call is running. Two other recent linear-time fixes in this project (the addressparser fallback for GHSA-v53p-9fqp-m79j and the DKIM header unfolding for GHSA-39m8-27wv-hr27) address entirely different modules and inputs and do not touch the AUTH mechanism regexes.

Affected Versions

  • Ecosystem: npm
  • Package: nodemailer
  • Confirmed affected range: >= 3.0.0, <= 10.0.12
  • Latest release checked: 10.0.12 (npm registry)
  • Fix status: 10.0.13

The four AUTH mechanism regexes were introduced when the SMTP client was bundled into nodemailer at 3.0.0 (previously a separate smtp-connection package). The vulnerable alternation (?:(\s+|=)[^\n]*\s+|\s+|=) is present, unchanged, in every published release from 3.0.0 (lib/smtp-connection/index.js) through 10.0.12 (dist/esm/smtp-connection/index.js and dist/cjs/smtp-connection/index.js). A later refactor added a leading [ -] character class but did not alter the ambiguous inner alternation. No release, and no development branch inspected at the current HEAD (30e4cfd), contains a fix for this pattern.

Suggested Fix

Replace the four backtracking regexes with a non-ambiguous parse of the AUTH extension. The invariant the fix must enforce is that mechanism detection runs in time linear in the response length regardless of whitespace shape. A minimal approach: match the AUTH extension value with a single non-backtracking pattern (for example, /[ -]AUTH(?:\s+|=)([^\r\n]*)/i) and then check for each mechanism name against the whitespace-split tokens with a Set lookup or includes. The fix must cover both continuation forms (250-AUTH ... and 250 AUTH ...) and both delimiters (space and =), and must handle the "AUTH advertised with no mechanisms" case without walking the whitespace run. As an interim mitigation, callers who never connect to an untrusted SMTP peer can restrict SMTP endpoints to a known allowlist; this does not help clients that must interoperate with arbitrary user-configured servers or with any cleartext SMTP path exposed to a network-adjacent attacker before STARTTLS.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

References

  • https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/security/advisories/GHSA-4ffr-jq9g-5ffx
  • https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/commit/b5a896fcb02df1628329d7cd665ca08490b14b56
  • https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/releases/tag/v10.0.13
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4ffr-jq9g-5ffx

entry.title: [nodemailer] Nodemailer: RFC 5322 comment inside an angle-bracket address is never stripped
entry.content:
Summary

Nodemailer's address parser has three published, patched fixes for RFC 5322 comment ( ... ) handling inside an addr-spec: GHSA-cc9r-2j5m-2m83 (comment glued two domain atoms into one), GHSA-g57g-f23g-4646 (the same glue for a quoted local part), and the related ReDoS fixes GHSA-prgh-xp8r-p3m5 / GHSA-v53p-9fqp-m79j. All three fixes live in _handleAddress()'s joins / _recoverAddrSpec() logic in src/addressparser/index.ts, and that logic is exercised whenever the local text-accumulation path in the tokenizer runs.

That logic is never reached at all for the single most common way a recipient is written: a display name followed by an angle-bracket address, Name <local@domain>. When the input inside the angle brackets itself contains an RFC 5322 comment, e.g.

Legit User <user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com>

the comment is not recognized as an operator, is not stripped, and the parenthesis characters survive verbatim inside the parsed address. That value is used as-is for envelope.to and is written raw onto the wire in the RCPT TO SMTP command. I confirmed this end to end:

  • against nodemailer's own jsonTransport/streamTransport (envelope.to and the emitted To: header both carry the malformed value), and
  • against a real SMTP server (aiosmtpd), where the malformed value is fatal to the transaction (501 Syntax: RCPT TO: <address> [SP <mail-parameters>], all recipients rejected).

This reproduces unmodified on every version I tested from 6.9.16 through the current 10.0.12 HEAD, i.e. it predates and survives all three of the address-parser advisories above unchanged, because it is a different root cause in a code path those fixes never touch.

Root cause

1. The tokenizer has a single-slot operator stack

src/addressparser/index.ts, Tokenizer.checkChar():

} else if (!this.operatorExpecting && !this.inDomainLiteral && chr in this.operators) {
    this.node = { type: 'operator', value: chr };
    this.list.push(this.node);
    this.node = null;
    this.operatorExpecting = this.operators[chr];
    this.escaped = false;
    return;
}

(currently around line 670)

operatorExpecting is a single string, not a stack. Once < opens the address scope, operatorExpecting is set to '>'. The branch above that recognizes a new operator character (such as () is gated on !this.operatorExpecting, which is now false. So while inside <...>, a ( is never tokenized as an operator at all — it is just an ordinary character appended to the running text token, together with everything up to the next >. The RFC 5322 comment is not recognized, not entered, and not stripped: it rides straight through as literal text.

2. The _handleAddress state machine loses the address state on any operator boundary

src/addressparser/index.ts, inside _handleAddress() (currently around line 365-388):

switch (token.value) {
    case '<':
        state = 'address';
        insideQuotes = false;
        break;
    case '(':
        state = 'comment';
        insideQuotes = false;
        break;
    ...
    default:
        state = 'text';
        insideQuotes = false;
        break;
}

Even where a comment is recognized (outside angle brackets), closing it with ) falls through to default and resets state to 'text', not back to whatever state was active before the comment opened. This is why the fixed cases (bare address, quoted local part) only work at all: the leaked comment tail lands in the free-text bucket, where _recoverAddrSpec()/the ADDR_SPEC extraction logic can find and strip it. Inside <...>, none of that applies in the first place (point 1), so there is no text-bucket safety net to fall back on — the whole point 1/point 2 interaction is what makes the angle-bracket case categorically different from, and unprotected by, the three existing fixes.

3. The one existing safety net requires whitespace, and this value has none

_recoverAddrSpec() (currently around line 283) is the function all three prior fixes rely on to peel a clean addr-spec back out of a polluted value. Its very first line is:

function _recoverAddrSpec(data: { address: string; text: string }): void {
    if (!HAS_WHITESPACE.test(data.address)) {
        return;
    }
    ...

user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com contains no whitespace at all — the comment content x had none, and nothing in the angle-bracket path inserts any — so _recoverAddrSpec bails out immediately and never even looks at the value. There is no cleanup path for this shape.

Proof of Concept

Environment: Node.js, current master (commit 30e4cfd5902fd5da4d1bc76dc8e4bc92d288adef, package.json version 10.0.12), no special transport configuration required.

Parser-level confirmation

const addressparser = require('nodemailer/lib/addressparser');
console.log(addressparser('Legit User <user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com>'));
// [ { address: 'user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com', name: 'Legit User' } ]

Compare with the already-fixed, unbracketed form of the exact same bytes:

console.log(addressparser('user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com'));
// [ { address: 'user@good-corp.com', name: 'evil.com' } ]   <- correctly stripped

sendMail / envelope confirmation (jsonTransport, no network)

const nodemailer = require('nodemailer');

(async () => {
    const t = nodemailer.createTransport({ jsonTransport: true });
    const info = await t.sendMail({
        from: 'app@good-corp.com',
        to: 'Legit User <user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com>',
        subject: 'hi',
        text: 'x'
    });
    console.log('envelope.to:', info.envelope.to);
})();

Observed output:

envelope.to: [ 'user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com' ]

The raw streamTransport message shows the same value in the emitted header:

From: app@good-corp.com
To: Legit User <user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com>
Subject: hi

Wire-level confirmation against a real SMTP server

const net = require('net');
const nodemailer = require('nodemailer');

const server = net.createServer(sock => {
    let buf = '';
    sock.write('220 sink ESMTP\r\n');
    sock.on('data', d => {
        buf += d;
        let i;
        while ((i = buf.indexOf('\r\n')) >= 0) {
            const line = buf.slice(0, i);
            buf = buf.slice(i + 2);
            const u = line.toUpperCase();
            if (u.startsWith('EHLO')) sock.write('250-sink\r\n250 8BITMIME\r\n');
            else if (u.startsWith('MAIL')) sock.write('250 ok\r\n');
            else if (u.startsWith('RCPT')) { console.log('wire RCPT TO :', line); sock.write('250 ok\r\n'); }
            else if (u.startsWith('DATA')) sock.write('354 go\r\n');
            else if (line === '.') sock.write('250 ok\r\n');
            else if (u.startsWith('QUIT')) { sock.write('221 bye\r\n'); sock.end(); }
            else sock.write('250 ok\r\n');
        }
    });
});

server.listen(0, '127.0.0.1', async () => {
    const t = nodemailer.createTransport({ host: '127.0.0.1', port: server.address().port, secure: false });
    const info = await t.sendMail({ from: 'app@good-corp.com', to: 'Legit User <user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com>', subject: 'hi', text: 'x' });
    console.log('envelope.to:', info.envelope.to);
    t.close(); server.close();
});

Observed:

wire RCPT TO : RCPT TO:<user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com>
envelope.to: [ 'user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com' ]

The same recipient string sent at a real, conformant SMTP server (aiosmtpd, a widely used reference-grade Python SMTP implementation) instead of the sink above:

Error: Can't send mail - all recipients were rejected: 501 Syntax: RCPT TO: <address> [SP <mail-parameters>]
code: 'EENVELOPE', responseCode: 501, command: 'RCPT TO',
rejected: [ 'user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com' ]

So against a strict receiver the immediate, concretely demonstrated outcome is that the message is bounced: an ordinary-looking recipient address that a sender/application believes is valid (and, see below, that some app-side validators do read as valid, at good-corp.com) silently fails to send.

Interpretation-conflict confirmation (same class as GHSA-cc9r-2j5m-2m83)

The same string, read by two other parsers an application might use to gate on the recipient's domain, produces two more, mutually different readings:

>>> import email.utils
>>> email.utils.parseaddr('Legit User <user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com>')
('Legit User (x)', 'user@good-corp.comevil.com')

>>> import email.policy, email.parser
>>> msg = email.parser.Parser(policy=email.policy.default).parsestr(
...     'To: Legit User <user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com>\n\n')
>>> addr = msg['To'].addresses[0]
>>> addr.username, addr.domain
('user', 'good-corp.com')

So for the exact same bytes:

Parser Domain read
Python email.utils.parseaddr good-corp.comevil.com (attacker-registrable)
Python email.policy.default (defects not inspected) good-corp.com (clean, would pass an allow-list check)
Nodemailer addressparser (this report) good-corp.com(x)evil.com (illegal characters, rejected by a strict MTA)

This is the exact "which parser sees what" comparison table from GHSA-cc9r-2j5m-2m83, reproduced through a different, unpatched code path: an application validating with email.policy.default without checking .defects (a documented pattern in that advisory) approves good-corp.com and hands the string to Nodemailer, which then emits a different, malformed value on the wire.

Version range

The built addressparser/sendMail output was tested for this exact input across published releases:

Version envelope.to
6.9.16 user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com
9.0.6 user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com
9.1.0 (fixed GHSA-cc9r-2j5m-2m83) user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com
10.0.1 user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com
10.0.12 / current HEAD (fixed GHSA-g57g-f23g-4646) user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com

Unchanged across every one of the three address-parser advisory fixes, because none of them touch the tokenizer's single-slot operatorExpecting state or the _handleAddress state-machine reset on ).

Impact

  • Confirmed, demonstrated impact: a recipient address that contains a perfectly legal RFC 5322 comment inside angle brackets — the single most common way a To/Cc/Bcc/From/Reply-To value is written (Display Name <user@domain>) — is parsed into a value containing SMTP-illegal characters ((, )) that a conformant receiving SMTP server rejects outright, silently failing message delivery to what the sender/application believed was a valid, already-validated recipient (CWE-20, availability/reliability impact on outbound mail).
  • Demonstrated interpretation conflict (CWE-436): the malformed value that reaches envelope.to and the wire RCPT TO command disagrees with how other parsers, including ones explicitly called out as an at-risk validation pattern in GHSA-cc9r-2j5m-2m83 (Python's email.policy.default without defect inspection), read the exact same bytes. An application gating outbound mail on "is the recipient's domain in my allow-list" using such a validator can approve a value that Nodemailer then sends corrupted, and depending on the receiving MTA's own comment handling, a different domain than either the sender or the validator believed was being used.
  • Reachability: every code path that ends up calling MimeNode._parseAddresses() — to, cc, bcc, from, replyTo, and the explicit envelope option — is affected identically, since they all funnel through the same addressparser()/_handleAddress() logic.

Suggested fix

The underlying issue is architectural: Tokenizer.operatorExpecting is a single value, so it cannot represent "currently inside an angle-address, and also currently inside a comment nested within it." A minimal fix is to make the tokenizer maintain a stack of expected closing characters (pushing ')' when entering a comment while another operator scope, e.g. '>', is already open, and popping back to the outer expectation on )), so a comment can be recognized and stripped no matter what scope it is nested inside. _handleAddress's state machine would then need to restore the previous state on a comment close instead of unconditionally resetting to 'text', so recognized-but-stripped comment content inside <...> continues to accumulate as address rather than leaking into text.

As defense in depth, _recoverAddrSpec() (or an equivalent check run specifically on data.address for the angle-bracket case) should also reject/clean any parsed address value that still contains RFC 5322 special characters such as (/) regardless of whether whitespace is present, since envelope.to is used directly to build an SMTP command and any character outside Mailbox (RFC 5321 §4.1.2) reaching that string is already the wrong outcome, independent of how it got there.

Regression test suggestion

Name <user@example.com(x)evil.com> and the bcc/cc/from/replyTo/envelope equivalents should all parse to { address: 'user@example.com', name: 'Name evil.com' } or be rejected outright by sendMail, never silently carry (/) into envelope.to.

References

  • https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/security/advisories/GHSA-g73g-hqqh-jr95
  • https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/commit/a502247555fd81773eac337486781f3b6008e16a
  • https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/releases/tag/v10.0.13
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g73g-hqqh-jr95

entry.title: [nodemailer] Nodemailer: Quadratic (O(n^2)) SMTP client reply parsing lets a malicious server or MITM cause a pre-auth remote denial of service
entry.content:
Summary

The SMTP client response parser reassembles multiline server replies by appending each continuation line onto a single response-queue entry and re-testing whether that entry is still a partial (continuation) reply on every line. The partial-response test runs str.slice(str.lastIndexOf('\n') + 1) on the growing entry, which forces a full flatten of the entire accumulated string on each line. A malicious or compromised SMTP server (or an on-path attacker on a plaintext or pre-STARTTLS hop) that streams continuation lines and never sends a completion line drives O(n^2) CPU on the single-threaded Node.js event loop before any authentication, freezing the whole process for an attacker-controlled duration.

Root Cause

The invariant that a server cannot cause superlinear client-side work while a reply is being reassembled is violated. In src/smtp-connection/index.ts, _onData splits inbound bytes into lines and, while the last queued entry is a continuation reply, concatenates each new line onto that same entry with this._responseQueue[len - 1] += '\n' + lines[i]. On every iteration it calls isPartialResponse(lastline), which evaluates /^\d+-/.test(str.slice(str.lastIndexOf('\n') + 1)). Because the queued entry grows by one line per continuation line and is stored as a V8 rope (ConsString), each lastIndexOf/slice forces a full string flatten of length proportional to the accumulated reply. Executed once per line over n continuation lines, this is O(n^2) CPU. While the reply stays partial the function early-returns and never resets the entry, so the growth and the per-line reflatten continue unbounded. There is no response-size or line-count cap in the connection code; the only limits are time-based (greetingTimeout, and an inactivity socketTimeout), and neither bounds accumulated reply size.

Affected file and functions (verified at the published v10.0.9 artifact, in src/ and in the built dist/cjs and dist/esm output):
- src/smtp-connection/index.ts: isPartialResponse (the /^\d+-/ test over str.slice(str.lastIndexOf('\n')+1))
- src/smtp-connection/index.ts: SMTPConnection._onData (the continuation-line append loop with no size cap)

Impact

An attacker who is, or can impersonate, the SMTP peer the client connects to can freeze the connecting Node.js process. Because Node.js is single-threaded, event-loop starvation halts all other work in that process (every other connection, request, and timer), not just the offending SMTP session. The reply is parsed during the greeting and EHLO phases, before the client authenticates or issues any command, so no credentials on the client are required. The blocking duration scales with the volume of continuation data the attacker streams and can be sustained indefinitely by continuing to stream, and memory for the accumulated entry also grows without bound. Independent reproduction on Node.js 24 measured roughly 11.6 seconds of event-loop blocking for about 640 KB of continuation data and roughly 47 seconds for about 1.3 MB, scaling quadratically. This is a repeatable remote denial of service against the sending process.

Proof of Concept

Node.js 24; a raw TCP listener acting as a hostile SMTP server; the client uses the shipped SMTPConnection (require('nodemailer/lib/smtp-connection')).

Steps: (1) start a TCP server that accepts a connection and streams continuation lines of the form 220-flood...\r\n in large batches, never emitting a completion line such as 220 ready; (2) point an SMTPConnection at it and observe the client event loop stall while the single response-queue entry grows and is reflattened on every line. A minimal microbenchmark of the exact parsing logic demonstrates the complexity:

// Reproduces isPartialResponse + the _onData append loop verbatim (Node 24).
function isPartialResponse(str) { return /^\d+-/.test(str.slice(str.lastIndexOf('\n') + 1)); }
function run(n) {
    const queue = [];
    let remainder = '';
    function onData(chunk) {
        const lines = (remainder + chunk).split(/\r?\n/);
        remainder = lines.pop();
        for (let i = 0; i < lines.length; i++) {
            if (queue.length && isPartialResponse(queue[queue.length - 1])) {
                queue[queue.length - 1] += '\n' + lines[i];
                continue;
            }
            queue.push(lines[i]);
        }
    }
    let buf = '';
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) buf += '220-flood line ' + i + '\r\n';
    const t = Date.now();
    onData(buf);
    return Date.now() - t;
}
for (const n of [8000, 16000, 32000, 64000]) console.log(n, run(n) + 'ms');

8000   26.5ms
16000  357.6ms
32000  2712.0ms
64000  11645.1ms
(2x input yields roughly 4x-7x time: quadratic. ~640 KB of continuation data blocks the event loop ~11.6s.)

Attack Chain

  1. Exposure: The client opens an SMTP connection whose peer is attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced: a compromised or malicious configured server, a tenant-supplied outbound server in a multi-tenant "bring your own SMTP" deployment, a deliverability or mailbox-probing tool that connects to arbitrary servers, or an on-path attacker on a plaintext or pre-STARTTLS hop.
  2. Control: The peer fully controls the bytes of its greeting and EHLO replies, including whether a reply ever completes.
  3. Path: Inbound bytes reach the socket data handler _onData, the sole data handler; every reply phase traverses the same continuation-append loop.
  4. Guard: No response-size or line-count cap exists. The greeting timer is time-based and cleared after the greeting, and its callback is itself starved while _onData runs synchronously; the inactivity timer resets on every inbound chunk, so an actively streaming attacker never trips it.
  5. Primitive: Each continuation line appended to the single growing queue entry triggers a full string flatten in isPartialResponse, yielding O(n^2) synchronous CPU on the event loop.
  6. Result: Whole-process event-loop starvation for an attacker-controlled, sustainable duration, plus unbounded memory growth: a remote denial of service reachable before authentication.

Bypass Evidence

The relevant guard would be a cap on accumulated reply size or line count. A search of the connection module (maxSize, maxLength, responseQueue.length >, byte or line ceilings) finds none; the only bounds are greetingTimeout and the inactivity-based socketTimeout, both time-based and neither bounding accumulated size. Disproof attempts: the greeting timeout does not help because it is time-based, fires only during the greeting phase, is cleared once the greeting completes, and its callback is delayed while _onData runs synchronously; a well-behaved server does not trigger the issue because a completion line resets the entry and keeps cost linear, but the modeled attacker is a hostile peer; segmented delivery does not help the defender because the response queue and line remainder persist across _onData calls so the accumulation and quadratic cost survive chunking; there is no safer alternate caller because _onData is the only data handler and the append loop is on every reply phase. Note on scope: core nodemailer connects to a configured host and does not perform MX resolution, so this is not reachable through a direct-to-MX transport; the malicious-peer, multi-tenant tenant-supplied-host, deliverability-probe, and MITM paths establish reachability.

Affected Versions

  • Ecosystem: npm
  • Package: nodemailer
  • Confirmed affected range: <= 10.0.9
  • Latest release checked: nodemailer 10.0.9 (npm registry; vulnerable code verified at git tag v10.0.9 and in the published dist output)
  • Fix status: 10.0.10

The quadratic reassembly shape is long-standing and predates the addressparser complexity fix family, so the exact introducing release is not positively established and the lower bound is left open; the upper bound is verified against the current published artifact, which is vulnerable with no fix.

Suggested Fix

Enforce that reassembling a multiline reply is linear in the reply size and that the reply size is bounded. Track the running length of the accumulated entry and the continuation state without re-scanning the whole entry on every line (for example, test the newly arrived line rather than slicing the tail of the growing accumulator, or collect lines in an array and join once at completion). Independently, impose a configurable maximum on the accumulated reply size or continuation-line count and fail the connection when it is exceeded, so a peer that never completes a reply cannot force unbounded work or memory. The remediation must cover every reply phase (greeting, EHLO, and command responses), because all of them flow through the same handler. As an interim mitigation, only connect to trusted SMTP servers over authenticated TLS (avoiding plaintext or STARTTLS-strippable hops), and in multi-tenant deployments isolate outbound SMTP sessions to tenant-supplied hosts so one tenant cannot starve a shared process.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).
